MR. NIELSEN-REQUEST FOR APPEARANCE BEFORE DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting, I believe, the institution of parliament and certainly all hon. members of this house. I rise to bring this matter to the attention of Your Honour, and to the attention of the government and the Prime Minister as the guardian of the rights of parliament itself and of the individual members thereof.
I want to say immediately in connection with the proceedings of the Dorion inquiry established by parliament that I am still of the same view that I expressed on November 25 and which appears in Hansard for that date, namely that I would be willing to assist the inquiry in any way I could. However, I believe that proprieties must be observed and that the rights of parliament and the members thereof must be preserved.
As far as I am aware from my research, no Canadian precedent can be found relating to the matter that I now raise. I have received by way of my solicitor, Mr. R. A. Bell, Q.C. of this city, a letter which I will read to the house. The letter is signed by Andre Desjardins, commission counsel of the special public inquiry, 1964. It is dated March 17, 1965 and is as follows:
Dear Sir:
As mentioned in our phone conversation of the 17 of March, I would like Mr. Erik Nielsen to appear before the commission next Tuesday, March the 23rd. It appears in the reports of the House of Commons Debates that Mr. Nielsen has stated that he has further information about the things that we are dealing with at the inquiry and that he would be willing to appear before the commission.
I take it, Mr. Speaker, that reference is to the debates of November 23.
I would like to question him on this subject, and I also understand that other counsels may wish to question him on an interview with Mr. Pierre Lamontagne a few days before November 23.
I remain,
Yours truly,
Andr6 Desjardins
Commission counsel
12S56

Question of Privilege
This, Mr. Speaker, is the first official intimation I have had that it is the intention of counsel to request that I appear before the commission. I do not wait for the issuance of an official subpoena because I do not wish to appear in the least reluctant to assist the commission in any way I can. But I do believe that the receipt of this letter, coming as it does from the official commission counsel, is sufficient upon which to base the privilege which I place now before the house.
I draw to Your Honour's attention a rule which I do not intend to more than refer to in passing, namely standing order 5. Further, in Beauchesne is found reference to the law of parliament which, as I see it, stipulates that no member is at liberty to give evidence elsewhere in relation to any debates or proceedings in parliament except by leave of the house of which he is a member.

maintopic: MR. NIELSEN-REQUEST FOR APPEARANCE BEFORE DORION COMMISSION
speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: MR. NIELSEN-REQUEST FOR APPEARANCE BEFORE DORION COMMISSION
speechtext:
I have no doubt, sir, that all members would willingly grant that consent. That will be developed, but I think the matter goes deeper than that. I believe the government must consider the introduction of a formal motion in order to give me that authorization to appear and discuss matters which have been raised in this house.
In respect of that statement of my understanding of the law of parliament, sir, I should like Your Honour to refer to the report of the United Kingdom select committee quoted in Beauchesne's fourth edition at pages 417 and 423. I should also like to refer Your Honour to May's fifteenth edition at page 121 and the case therein cited. I believe this ruling also applies to officers of the house, and in that connection it is my understanding that one of the officers of the house, the present Clerk, has had an experience in that regard.
May's fifteenth edition at page 121 sets out the following:
Members of both houses are, by the law and custom of parliament, exempted from attendance as witnesses during the session of parliament, and from service as jurors at all times by the Juries Act. 1870 (see p. 77).
But, according to present usage, the service of a subpoena on a member during the session of parliament, unless effected within the precincts of the house, sedente domo (see p. 77) would not, as a general rule, be regarded as a breach of privilege.
The reference in Beauchesne to which I referred Your Honour includes the following statement at page 423, in paragraph 11:
By the law of parliament "no member is at liberty to give evidence elsewhere in relation to any

debates or proceedings in parliament, except by the leave of the house of which he is a member": and no clerk or officer of the house or shorthand writer employed to take minutes of evidence before the house or any committee thereof may give evidence elsewhere in respect of any proceedings or examination had at the bar or before any committee of the house without the special leave of the house.
It is to that reference that I draw Your Honour's attention.
The Dorion commission, or one of its officers by the authority of the commission, sir, has already directed members of the house to appear and testify before it. Two members of the house have in fact appeared before the commission and have testified. I may be incorrect in stating this, sir, but I believe that neither the permission of Your Honour nor any special leave of the house in accordance with the rules was granted to either of those members who did in fact appear before the commission. One of them is a minister of the crown. The directions or requests to the members of the house to appear before the commission were not and have not been communicated, to my knowledge, to Your Honour. While the rules may have been overlooked in that regard, I believe that is still a breach of what I believe to be parliamentary law. The members who appeared and testified did so without first having obtained the consent of the house so to do, which is also contrary to parliamentary law.
I understand also, sir, that the list of witnesses which has been published in the press is an indication of an intention to again call one minister of the crown and the Minister of Justice before the inquiry. I believe in reply to a question put by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition the Prime Minister indicated that he too would be willing to appear before the inquiry if a subpoena were issued to him.
I believe, sir, that the question I raised is one which should be given serious consideration by the house. It is my understanding after reading the precedents that a substantive motion should be introduced granting special leave to any member of the house to attend this or any other judicial proceeding while parliament is in session.
I raise the matter now, at the first indication I have had from the commission that it is intended to request that I testify before it. The week end is coming up. The Prime Minister and his government will have an opportunity to consider the question of privilege involved, and it would be my suggestion to

him that a substantive motion be introduced by the government authorizing me to attend before the commission.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

I want to do things in a proper manner and in accordance with the rules, and I am sure that members will appreciate the proprieties involved here. It will not take much effort to prepare a motion to which I am sure all hon. members would agree, authorizing me to appear and giving me that special leave referred to in the rules to discuss matters which have been raised in the house.
I put this question before you, sir. I believe it is the responsibility of the government to introduce such a motion. It may well be that other procedures are available, but my own research of the rules does not indicate this to be so.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNCONDITIONAL GRANT OF $10 MILLION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNCONDITIONAL GRANT OF $10 MILLION
speechtext:
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to make a statement on the financing of the Canada Council which was set up in 1957 to foster and promote in Canada the arts, humanities and the social sciences.
The council is financed by an endowment fund of $50 million. Its relationship to parliament is through the public accounts committee, which each year examines its annual report. Since 1957 there has been no significant change in the council's sources of income other than a gratifying appreciation in the value of its investments. Meanwhile, however, the needs it was established to meet have grown rapidly. The prestige and value of the council have also grown in the steps it has taken to meet these needs.
With its present income the council is restricted to affording only minimal assistance in the creation and development of new artistic resources to meet the needs of the future. In the humanities and social sciences the council has had to adopt restrictive measures, particularly in the award of scholarships and fellowships. There is clear requirement for an enlarged-not a reduced -program of assistance in this field.
For these reasons the government has decided that the council's income should be increased. We believe that the best long term method of achieving this result would be to increase the endowment fund, because it fully protects the independence of the council. We feel however, that it would be unwise to take this course under present circumstances. For one thing, the Canadian universities foundation is now making a study of the needs of universities, including their requirements in the fields of the humanities and the social sciences. This report will not be available before the end of 1965. Also there have been suggestions that the Canada Council might be divided and a new special agency created for the humanities and social sciences. This is a matter which requires the most careful consideration. A hasty decision would clearly be unwise, and even if a change were to be made it would

Canada Council
take some considerable time for it to be implemented.
These and other factors contribute to make the future needs of the council difficult to estimate. This is why the government has decided to propose a temporary measure of assistance. According to section 20 of the act the council is entitled to receive donations to be used for the general purposes set out in section 8. Accordingly we intend to include in the final supplementary estimates for the current fiscal year an unconditional grant of $10 million which will enable the Canada Council to meet its minimum foreseeable requirements during the next few years. We know this money will be well spent and will serve to promote the arts, the humanities and the social sciences at a time when it has become imperative to foster Canada's development in these fields and thus strengthen the identity and the unity of our country as we approach our centennial.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNCONDITIONAL GRANT OF $10 MILLION
speechtext:
While no notice was given in advance that this matter would be raised, this is one occasion when I think there will be general agreement with the course of action suggested.
I realize the difficulties under which the Canada Council operates. With the money it has had available it has done a great deal to advance the arts, the social sciences and the humanities. Just how serious is the question of higher education is shown by a telegram which I received shortly before I came into the house. It sets out the attitude of mind on the part of the student bodies of the universities in the maritime provinces, which is a matter of great concern in other parts of Canada. I will read only the portions of the telegram that set out the material matters I have in mind:
Concerning the unnecessary increase in university fees, announced Tuesday, March 16, 1965, by the association of Atlantic universities, the student union of Mount Allison University deplores this untimely action, especially when the report of the Bladen commission on higher education and the results of the Canadian student means survey have not yet been released...
The students of this university are prepared to exact every pressure possible. Presently Mount Allison has the highest undergraduate tuition fees in the maritime area, a situation which we feel is completely unjustified in light of the economic difficulties of the region. The student union of Mount Allison is taking the immediate action of calling a maritime regional conference of the Canadian union of students at this university in order that a detailed brief may be forwarded to the provincial and federal governments. Furthermore, the directors of the association of maritime students are meeting Saturday, March 20, 1965. at the University of Moncton in order that immediate action be taken.

We strongly suggest that the federal government place this grave matter on the order paper in the House of Commons for immediate consideration, as this is an urgent matter of regional and national interest. Students do not feel that they can bear the result which will definitely prove disastrous to the principles of higher education-
That is signed by William Allison Pinkney. The Prime Minister mentioned the question of the expansion of scholarships and fellowships by the Canada Council. I think that is a worthy objective. The Canada Council must have the necessary funds in order to permit the widest possible extension of the opportunities of university education. That brings me, in the most kindly way also, to ask where are the 10,000 scholarships that we heard so much about two or three years ago.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNCONDITIONAL GRANT OF $10 MILLION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNCONDITIONAL GRANT OF $10 MILLION
speechtext: Certainly $10 million will not make provision for that expansive policy as promised. I think, in general, that when the supplementary estimates come up this matter can then be discussed in detail. In the meantime I have brought to the attention of the Prime Minister this telegram, which I believe represents a serious situation. After all, if our Canadian university students have to pay these increased fees, ultimately it will be this nation that will suffer if the numbers of prospective students are reduced because of inability to attend university though possessing the intellectual qualifications that would assure a greater contribution by them in the years ahead.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNCONDITIONAL GRANT OF $10 MILLION
speechtext:
We think this is a very good step, Mr. Speaker, and that the government will receive a very favourable response across the country with regard to it. I suggest to the Prime Minister that some of us may be somewhat surprised at the idea of splitting the humanities and social sciences from the Canada Council. Certainly one of the saddest things about the Canada Council and the concept that really Mr. Brooke Clax-ton had of it is that the endowment part has not really been supported in a wide way. We had the rather ironical situation with the first really substantial grant that came from private funds to the Canada Council, in that it was for certain fields of endeavour for which the Canada Council really had not considered it was responsible. That particular endowment, devoted to medicine, science and engineering in the main, in a sense expanded the scope of the Canada Council's activities beyond what had been contemplated.

I myself and some other colleagues felt that this may have been wrong; that maybe the idea should have been to establish another aspect of the Canada Council to deal with these fields and to leave the Canada Council for humanities and social sciences and support in what you might call the general arts subjects. The idea of a grant to the endowment fund would have interested us largely because of the success of the Canada Council in keeping this endowment fund in good shape and earning a rate of interest from it that would compare quite favourably with what private organizations are doing. This is one of the reasons we think further consideration of the endowment idea would be worth while.
I would like to compliment the Minister of Finance in connection with this program, because I imagine that an unconditional grant of this size coming at the end of the session is an indication that either he has relented or he has approved the project; and I would like to take it as an indicator that there is at least one member of the cabinet who is favourable to further support for universities.
With regard to the matter referred to by the Leader of the Opposition, it fits rather awkwardly into this announcement at this particular time, but I certainly feel that the point raised by the telegram from the students of Mount Allison is one that the government now has a responsibility for, in view of the fact that the government has the student loans fund in existence on such a large scale. If that student loans fund is to become in a sense the forerunner or the opening of the door for universities to run up their fees in any uncontrolled way, it really means that the students and the federal government in a sense are becoming one more and rather odd way in which universities finance themselves.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF UNCONDITIONAL GRANT OF $10 MILLION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that few people will object to increasing the funds at the disposal of the Canada Council, even if the increase only amounts to $10 million. We know that such grants are necessary especially in the field of arts. Even with those $10 million and much more money, it would be impossible to satisfy everybody.
Although I do not have the Canada Council annual report here, I understand that several candidates complained that they could not obtain the scholarships they were entitled to while several persons thought that other candidates who did not seem to be serious candidates obtained them.
Canada Council
I take this opportunity to say how much I am in favour of the recommendation of the committee on procedure and organization requesting the establishment of a standing committee on cultural affairs so that we can, not only intervene directly in the administration of the Canada Council, but at least take a look at the guide lines, the basic principles of that agency's policy.
If I remember correctly, we were told that the Canada Council made fairly large income producing investments in order to support and assist various people who applied for scholarships. And if I am not mistaken, last year the Canada Council stated in its report that it had granted loans to various companies, including finance companies. Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) tells us that a special amount is to be granted or given the Canada Council for the purpose of assisting the arts and the humanities. I also heard the right hon. Prime Minister talk about increasing scholarships for special studies.
In view of the fact that the Canada Council grants many scholarships for special studies in this country, I would suggest that our Canadian artists benefit more therefrom. I believe that the council has a large amount of work ahead, and it should assist to a greater extent the performing arts.
We have a great number of artists, many talented opera singers who were applauded in New York, Buenos Aires, San Francisco, at the Scala of Milan, the Vienna Opera; we also have others who belong to the Sadler's Wells Ballet, but unfortunately in Canada we still lack a professional and permanent opera company.
We have musicians who belong to symphonic orchestras in every country, but our orchestras are still lacking in that financial assistance which would allow them to prosper. We also have theatre groups which should be granted greater financial assistance, though our theatrical groups have benefited greatly since the establishment of the Canada Council.

Procedure Committee Report
I believe that the best recommendations we could make to the Canada Council would be to not only promote the training of artists but also assist in planning artistic manifestations.
It is not enough to have talents, for we can find them in the public; it is not enough to train them in Canada, they must have the opportunity to perform for the Canadian people. I think this would be the specific role of the Canada Council.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we hope that this is merely a temporary measure. But according to what the Prime Minister said, this temporary measure would become permanent before long. This is our hope also. With regard to scholarships for university students, about which some hon. members have already spoken in the house, Mr. Speaker, I think the Canada Council should be careful not to encroach on provincial autonomy in the field of education. It is recognized that education comes under the provinces. In my opinion, the Canada Council should respect the provincial autonomy in the matter of education.
At all events we hope the government will increase its assistance and grants to our artists, that it will put more money at the disposal of our artists, our classical scholars, our poets, our composers and others, so that the artistic, literary and cultural life may flourish in our country and that our people may enjoy henceforth a more active cultural life.

Procedure Committee Report as I am concerned, I believe the special committee that was set up on procedure and organization was given a specific task. That committee, after having made an inquiry, has come back to this house with certain recommendations, and it has completed its job up to a point.

Prime Minister yesterday, as well as the speeches made by the hon. member for Peace River and other members who have contributed to this debate. However, we have not solved the procedural problem with which we are faced at this moment. Whether or not there was a general agreement among house leaders and members of the committee, we must recognize that such an agreement cannot be extended to cover what we now require, and that is unanimous consent. For that reason I feel we should consider citation 322 in Beauchesne's fourth edition, which appears at page 251 and is as follows:
When the motion to concur is proposed-
This refers to a committee report.
-the report may be referred back to the committee for further consideration or with instruction to amend it in any respect.
The next part of the citation I believe to be extremely important, Mr. Speaker.
It is not competent for a committee to reconsider and reverse its own decision, but if the house resolves that such reconsideration is necessary, the correct procedure is for the house to give the committee instructions which will enable it to consider the whole question again.
It is my impression that in the speech made by the Prime Minister as well as in speeches made by other members there was an indication that some reconsideration is necessary, and I am sure the committee is prepared to carry out such reconsideration. How can we get around this matter of unanimous consent to either stand the debate or, for that matter -and I would be willing-to ask for unanimous consent to withdraw the motion? Again this would require unanimous consent, and if that is not forthcoming it seems the only way we can accomplish that which I believe most members wish to accomplish is by a motion to refer the report back to the committee for further consideration. This can be done, but it must come from the house unless we have unanimous consent either to withdraw or stand the motion. As far as the committee is concerned, there were some very useful suggestions made and I am sure we are prepared to deal with them, but citation 322 really obliges us to have some instruction from the house before amending this report.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the difference in the total amount of loans may be explained by the fact that the Quebec government assists the borrowers from that province by paying the interest on loans granted under the farm credit legislation; this does not apply to other provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion for concurrence in this report was moved yesterday in accordance with what I thought was the general wish of the house that there would be a one day debate on the report, that one day of course to be a full day and not a Wednesday or a Friday. We proceeded throughout the day and had a rather useful and extensive debate. Near the conclusion of the debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) dealt with the report in a fairly comprehensive way and indicated the importance that the government attached to many of the recommendations in the report. He then went on to indicate that he would welcome the changes in the standing orders that would achieve the objectives set out in part of the report. He had already dealt with other things not in the report, had indicated their importance and had gone on to indicate with regard to two of the changes in the report, one having to do with the committee structure and the other having to do with the desirability of referral of estimates to committees, that they were substantial changes and that he hoped something could be done to bring forward actual standing orders that could be considered by the house and either accepted or rejected. In any event, the point I want to make is that he indicated the importance and urgency that the government attaches to this matter.
I had assumed, maybe wrongly but certainly my assumption was based on general

discussions, that it would be agreeable that after a day's debate had taken place, the matter would be left for later consideration. Since it is an interim report only and not a final report, the committee has full authority to go ahead. Because I had understood from conversations with committee members that they in their turn were willing and anxious to go ahead, I believed that the committee should refine their suggestions further, in a way that would involve the presenting of specific standing orders for consideration by the house. In any event, as was demonstrated this morning, my assumption was wrong.
In the circumstances in which we find ourselves, we are now at a stage where I think all hon. members will agree that we are seeking to bring this session to a termination and get on with the new session, and the government has indicated only a very few items of government business that have to be finished. We have in fact discussed at some length the exact procedure for terminating this session and starting the new one. In the light of that, I do not propose at the moment to enter into a discussion of the report in detail, much as I should like to do so. Rather, I should like to repeat what I said this morning by way of a point of order when this motion was first called.
I sought then to bring about some agreeable conclusion to the debate on this report, a conclusion agreeable to the main body of opinion in the house and, I hope, acceptable to all others who might not be in full agreement with what was being done. I made one or two suggestions and those suggestions did not seem to find acceptability. I do not know whether or not they were worthy of it. In any event, they did not receive acceptability in the house.
I think there is a consensus among members of the house to go on to other business and I am prepared to move that the report be referred back for further consideration. In doing so, I want to state again, as I did on the point of order earlier, the concern of the government to make progress with any procedures or changes in the procedures that will improve the ability of the house to handle its business. I think that wish is shared by all hon. members. Since this is a committee matter and as I am not a member of the committee, it is not proper for me to say what the committee will do. But I have in mind their past history, the number of reports they have already made, this being the fifteenth, some of which have been very good and have resulted in action
Procedure Committee Report being taken. I know from conversations I have had that the committee members are anxious to proceed.
I am also sure that the government is willing to do anything it can reasonably and properly do by way of co-operation with the committee. If the committee feels there is anything the government can do by way of being of assistance, by having any of the ministers who have experience in procedural matters meet with the committee on behalf of the government or any other such step, the government would be willing to take it.
Since I am seeking to achieve an agreeable conclusion to this matter so that we can put this work in hand and get on with other work, I can do no better than move, seconded by the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
That the said report be not now concurred in, but that it be referred back to the said committee for further consideration of the recommendations outlined therein.
I think it will be noticed that the language is general because after what consultation I could have over the lunch hour I was not able to achieve any draftsmanship that I thought would more fairly and accurately enable the committee to consider what they sense to be the consensus of the house arising out of the discussion. I considered this form to be better than a specific, detailed type of motion. I hope my action in preventing this motion will commend itself to the house.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a couple of difficulties that I think should be apparent, but before we deal with them I think it should be pointed out in fairness to everyone who is interested in the committee report which I am sure includes all members of the house whether or not they have spoken on the matter, that the report was presented to the house before the Christmas recess. In addition, it was understood at that time that, primarily at the request of the government, the motion to adopt would be moved by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) only for the purpose of explaining to the house the full implications of the committee's thinking in regard to the report. The government wanted a period of time to elapse so that members of the house would be able to study the report in detail, which I am sure was done. When we resumed following the Christmas recess it was again at the request of the government that consideration of this report was postponed because there were other matters of concern to the country that needed to be dealt with.

Procedure Committee Report
One of those was the Canada pension plan. There was no inclination to interfere with the progress of the Canada pension plan. In fact, there was an intense desire on the part of members in the opposition, and in my own party which I know more intimately, to see the Canada pension plan proceeded with as quickly as possible so that it could become law in the nation. The situation therefore is not entirely as put by the President of the Privy Council. There are some other factors which I have just outlined, namely that the progress on this particular report and the motion attendant upon it has been to suit the convenience of the government almost entirely.
The motion before us is to refer the report back to the committee for reconsideration and study, at least of parts of it. If we are to take the words of the President of the Privy Council at their face value, and knowing that it is the desire of the government, indeed a necessity, to conclude this session as quickly as possible, then we may very well find ourselves in a position, by making this referral back to the committee, of having the committee disintegrate at the prorogation of this session. The committee only has life until the end of the session. We could very easily find ourselves in a position of having a report referred back to the committee although they may not have a chance to embark upon the re-examination. It may well be that the session will end, the committee will end and all the work the committee has put into this report will go down the drain. Presumably, when the session resumes the committee will have to start all over again, be reconstituted and have the subject matter referred to it again.
In one sense, the amendment placed before the house by the President of the Privy Council could very easily, if it is not designed for the purpose, have the effect of killing completely the ideas contained in the committee report. This, I do not want to see. Each person who spoke about the report has done so in glowing terms of the direction in which the committee is headed. There have been differences, there are bound to be differences, over the details as to whether or not this or that particular point is good or bad. However, in essence, everyone in the house, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), has spoken in favour of the general principle advanced by the committee. I am very much afraid that the amendment posed by the President of the Privy Council will


have the effect of destroying that intention, that hope, if there is an early prorogation of this session, or dissolution, whichever the case may be. Until a new committee is established in the following session we will be in a position of having nothing to reconsider. It would be a disaster if that occurred.
I feel that what should have occurred would have been for the government-I was hoping the Prime Minister would have done this-to go down the list of recommendations detail by detail and lay out clearly the desires and hopes of the government with respect to each one of them. Instead, the Prime Minister made a sort of catch-all speech in which he took bits and pieces of objections and tried to put them together, saying in a vague sort of way that the government would agree or disagree with certain things. The course I have advocated has not been followed by the government, and as a consequence parliament is now in the awkward position of having to kill proposals with which we all agree. This results from the minister's having moved the amendment that he has, coupled with the fact that this matter has been delayed persistently at the request of, and for the convenience of, the government itself.
If there is the chance that the committee will have an opportunity to examine further these and other related matters, then I think it should take cognizance of one simple factor, namely the difference of opinion that exists and that has always existed in parliament between the desires of the government and the desires of private members. There is this conflict between the desires of private members and their opportunity to function properly, and the desire of cabinet to have control over the procedures of parliament. We were hoping we could perhaps get out of this situation. Last evening the Prime Minister and other members who spoke spent almost their entire time looking at this report from the point of view of the advantages that would accrue to the government from it. They looked at it from the point of view of how it would enhance the position of the cabinet and give to the cabinet a greater degree of control over the operations of parliament.
I think what should occur to balance that is to have some consideration given by the committee to the position of private members in order to ensure, so far as possible, that the members of the opposition particularly, who are the most active private mem-

bers, will have the opportunity to fully examine government activities in detail and have an opportunity to get their points of view across, have them considered and dealt with *either by defeat or by passage, whatever the case may be. I believe this subject should be given a greater degree of consideration by the committee, namely, what can be done to alter the rules of parliament to enhance the position of the opposition, to give to it its rightful function and place in the parliament of Canada, to provide private members an opportunity to express their points of view and to have those points of view either rejected or accepted.
May I just make one reference here. Today is one of the days upon which public bills in the names of private members will be considered. The traditional approach, with some few exceptions, on the part of the government has been to treat these bills as a necessary evil, as a sort of exercise in debate. Persistently the approach has been, not only by this government but all governments over the years, to talk out private members' proposals-not to consider them on their merits, not to meet them head on, not to argue about a good or a bad proposition, but to talk out the propositions advanced by private members. This is something the committee should consider. How can we make changes in the rules to give opposition members, and government backbenchers, the opportunity to present their views and to have them met on the basis of the merits of the ideas themselves?
Perhaps one way to do this would be, automatically upon the introduction of a public bill by a private member, if it is in order and meets the other rules of the house, to have it referred to one of the standing committees where it could be examined on its merits, where individual members or cabinet ministers could argue for and against the bill. Perhaps a better approach would be to give to the committees that we seek to establish here the right to initiate legislation, to come up with ideas themselves. After all, Mr. Speaker, the concept that all the brains in Canada are in the heads of cabinet ministers is a foolish one. There are many brilliant members in this parliament who are not cabinet members, who have exceptionally good ideas, meritorious ideas which, if accepted, would advance the cause of democracy, the economic and social structure of this nation. But they do not have the opportunity to see those ideas presented and some conclusion reached about them.
Procedure Committee Report
I think also that we should make some other alterations in the committees structure, notably to give to the committees research facilities and research staffs. If we intend that all the estimates with one or two exceptions should be referred automatically to committees for examination we should give to those committees adequate facilities for examining them; we should provide them with staffs of statisticians, economists, lawyers and whoever else might be necessary to provide background information so that the committee may examine the proposed expenditures in detail. Right now the whole weight of the civil service of Canada, thousands upon thousands of experts, together with some who are not experts, is available for the purpose of assisting, guiding and advising the political head of a department. Against this mammoth structure there exists only the private member with whatever abilities he himself has and whatever research facilities he is able to rely on to give him advice and information about the operation of government departments. If we were to take action along the lines I am suggesting we would be enhancing the position of parliament in the mind of the average Canadian; we would be bringing parliamentary activity closer to the average Canadian; we would be providing not only for the proper study of the estimates to be made but we would be furnishing the necessary staff so that such studies could be carried out in depth, as well as providing an opportunity for public organizations, groups and individual citizens to present their ideas about particular proposals for government expenditure. These are among the questions which I hope the committee will examine if and when it has the chance to do so.
My hon. friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) yesterday made a special appeal to the government with regard to one phase of the committee's report, protesting against the lumping together of the three subjects of health, welfare and veterans affairs. As a consequence of this appeal, or perhaps independently of it, the Prime Minister agreed that veterans affairs should not be lumped together with health and welfare but that they should be considered by a committee specially designed to deal with them.
I wish I had known the outcome of the remarks made by my hon. friend from Kootenay West. I would have asked him to speak for others and make the same suggestion with regard to Indian affairs. Here, too, is a special group of people requiring special consideration, and to lump in the consideration of In-

Procedure Committee Report dian affairs with such subjects as the R.C.M.P., the criminal law, civil rights, prisons and all the other subjects which presumably come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice, as well as a whole field of matters relating to the operation of the citizenship and immigration branch, is in my view altogether unfair. However, following the eloquent submission which the hon. member for Kootenay West made yesterday I can only suggest that this is another subject which should be given special consideration and examined solely by a committee designed to examine the affairs of the Indian affairs branch, and the relationship of government with our native Indian people.
Members of this party who have spoken earlier in this discussion have stated that in general we are favourably disposed to the report of the committee. That is the position I take. I am not disposed to favour certain of the details but I am sure every hon. member has similar views with respect to certain of the detailed proposals which have been made. Somewhere along the line I think the government itself should have spelled out in detail the views it holds about these various proposals. After all, this matter has been delayed to suit the convenience of the government day after day since Christmas. Surely in that time the government could have produced some ideas indicating what it believed to be the most advantageous parts of this report, so that we might be dealing now with something conclusive. But because of the inaction, or inability, or lack of desire, or split which may exist within the Liberal party about this report we are faced with a distinct possibility of having to destroy that which we do not want to destroy-of having to kill something which each one of us would endorse in principle. I think it is a shame we should have got to such a stage when we are considering a question as vital as the operation of parliament, which is so fundamental to our approach to democracy.
I think it is regrettable that by continued procrastination on the part of the government as well as by this killing motion which the President of the Privy Council made today, we should find ourselves being asked to destroy that which we do not want to destroy. Somehow or other we have to extricate ourselves from this position.

I do not intend to speak at any length. However, last evening, I am informed, the hon. and attractive member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) appeared as a

news commentator, objective and unbiased, on the television program "Viewpoint", and expressed herself in a way which is not quite in keeping with what one might expect from her. She obviously presented only one side of the case-the government side of the case.

speechtext: I presented the facts.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: She gave the impression to the Canadian people that no one from the front bench of Her Majesty's loyal opposition had spoken.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Correct.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The reason for this, according to her interpretation, was opposition to the recommendations made.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Where were you yesterday?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I want to say at once that the hon. member is seldom so wide of the mark as she was last evening. I will say no more than this: Her objectivity was somewhat destroyed by the apparent bias which was shown. I say this in the greatest spirit of kindliness, having the highest regard for the hon. lady's intellectual attainments.
I wish to make it clear that the attitude of of the opposition is one of the fullest cooperation at all times in assuring that parliament shall remain effective. It is of interest that we are celebrating at this very moment the 700th anniversary of the foundation of parliament. Great celebrations will take place at Westminster in the month of June. But it is at this very time, between I believe the middle of February and the 20th of March, that the first parliament was convened in the United Kingdom. There was an earlier parliament in Iceland, but we in the British tradition think of the parliament of Simon de Montfort as constituting the beginnings of our parliamentary system.
All through the years there have been criticisms of this system. Much has been said about the need for reform. Cynics have always criticized this institution. Cynics today criticize the parliament of the United Kingdom as they did before and after the first world war and during and after the second world war. Yet that parliamentary system has been made effective-so effective that the voice of freedom was heard from Westminster all over the world. Whatever its shortcomings, parliament has been effective.
The hon. member who just resumed his seat made a very reasoned argument. He said we must guard against the possibility that the government-and all governments are

liuman-is most anxious to bring about changes in the rules that will assure to the greatest degree possible the least amount of debate from the opposition. So often we hear debate criticized as useless and as worthless. We have no filibuster under our system of government-

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-and yet the expression has found its way into the language of our country. Long debates are necessary when principle is at stake. We had the best example in the last few days of what debate will do. I speak of the hon. members to the far left of this chamber who took a strong and definite stand to make this parliament in fact bilingual, as it is constitutionally, a stand not only desirable but prescient. They were joined by the rest of us on this side of the house. With all the excuses which the government offered, finally the government had to capitulate. In other words, long debate brought about the necessary change in the thinking of a government that would have brushed this whole thing aside.
In my days as prime minister we brought about simultaneous translation. There were many who said, "Why bring this in?" My [DOT]contention was that parliament is and must remain bilingual and the only way to make it effective is through the instrumentality of a system such as that. I mention this because there was great criticism that parliament was being held up and the pension legislation was going to be destroyed because members in the opposition dared to stand for the rights of parliament. They stood. Excuses were given, all kinds of excuses, for not acting. The government had acted most cavalierly in its attitude when asked for a copy in the French language of the proceedings of the committee. Their request was ridiculed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss La-Marsh). Excuses were given that it would take four months-

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Four weeks.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-and finally it ends up that it is going to take a matter of four days. This just shows the effect of argument strongly held and contended for. I think of the story told of Lord Kitchener in South Africa in 1900, who called a group of generals together and said, "I want you to do such and so", and they spent an hour, two or three, saying it could not be done. Then he said, "Now that you have given me every reason why it could not be done, go and do it". That is
Procedure Committee Report what happened here. Parliament spoke, the opposition stood; and the government, surrounded by its own supporters, was silent or evasive.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, we want to make parliament efficient, and one thing that we must guard against is that we make the cabinet more powerful than it is. The trend in parliamentary government-as the hon. gentleman has said, and so well said- following two world wars has been to bring about an all-powerful executive, holding support oftentimes by that tremendous authority that is exercised by a prime minister of having it in his power to recommend a dissolution, which I am told has its effect in bringing recalcitrants to change their viewpoint, and very soon.

I said the cabinet is becoming all powerful, and one has only to see it in examples that we have from time to time. If these hon. gentlemen opposite could speak, what would they be saying about Mr. Rivard? What would they be saying-

But they don't say anything over there. We have not been able to find out even today whether they ever let the United States know about the reward.

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the degree to which objection is offered to what I am saying indicates that argument can be and is effective. That does not mean we should continue to follow rules that are no longer applicable to the complex nature of the

Procedure Committee Report problems that we face. I go back to 1879, and here is something that indicates the cynicism of that time. It appeared in "Grit" published in Toronto on February 15, 1879, and this particular member of the press gallery used these immortal words:
Yes, 'tis pleasant to think as I sit in the gallery,
They agree upon one thing and that is their salary.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is a cynical view that is held; but I am just pointing it out, not because of its applicability to today-far be it from me to think of that-but simply because as far back as 1879 it was stated that there was only one thing upon which we agreed. The parliament of the United Kingdom today is criticized as never before; all the parliaments in the British tradition have been. But we must always remember this, that in making changes we ought not simply to follow the theoretical idealism of some who with it have not the practical knowledge of years in public life. The objective which we all have in mind is to make parliament more effective. I am not going to reiterate what I have already said. Certainly my experience with committees has not led me to believe that, on any matter on which there is strong controversy or aroused partisan feeling, committees are divorced from

There is also a need for the fuller examination of the estimates. I have said on other occasions that a government could put $10 million in the estimates without there being, any justification of the item, and in the rush at the end of a session that item could be passed. This means it is quite impossible for members to carry out and discharge their other responsibilities, at the same time giving to the examination of supply, which is the first responsibility of parliament, the attention it deserves. Anything that will bring about improvement in the examination of supply will at all times command my support, in fact my enthusiastic support.
I do not agree with the suggestion that because recommendations will seem radical they are therefore necessarily beneficial. If there is one thing you have been able to dof Mr. Speaker-and I say this with great respect __it is that you have been able to give to parliament, through the assistance and counsel you have given, a degree of importance to this committee that few committees have enjoyed in this house. There is one matter to which I wish to make reference, however, and I do not believe in being diplomatic regarding a matter you cannot accept. I am concerned over paragraph 23 of the report:
Your committee is of the opinion that the effectiveness of parliament would be improved if the house were to adjourn for certain periods during which committees would be able to meet for a week at a time...Your committee therefore recommends that the house should adjourn at regular intervals for two weeks at a time in order to accomplish-

Mr. Speaker, in my remarks on the committee report I do not intend to mention Lucien Rivard or bilingualism at all. However, it has become more than abundantly clear that there will be no unanimous consent to agree to the amendment proposed by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith), and as speakers before me have said, the effect of the passage of this amendment would be to kill the work of the committee for the present time. I cannot conceive that the committee could carry out a proper study, do the research and report back again before prorogation of this session, and this would mean the end of the work of that committee.
Had the government's amendment not been so general, and had there been some specific recommendations, I think it might have received wide support in the house. Personally I have found that the report almost in its entirety is a good one and I see no particular reason why it should go back; but rather than see it defeated in this house, this seems to me to be the next best thing. However, as I have said, I do not think the motion should have been made in such general terms.
If all the recommendations of the committee had been accepted, certainly there would be a vast improvement in the committees system of the house. I think hon. members should not delude themselves by thinking that if all the recommendations had been accepted we would not still be a long way from having a congressional type of committee.
Everyone in the house has expressed concern about the growth of the power of the executive in parliament during the past few years. This is common in Canada, the United Kingdom and in all parliamentary democracies. Everyone has expressed concern about the growth of the executive and a weakening of the power of a private member; however, no one really does very much about this. I suggest that changes would be difficult to effect. It seems to me that no cabinet in a parliamentary democracy would really want to see very much change, because by the measure of the increase in private members' powers, and by the measure of the strength of committees, the power of the cabinet is

Procedure Committee Report reduced, and a cabinet is not likely to want that. That is only a human feeling and I think it is true of almost any cabinet in power. It is difficult to reconcile the growing strength on the part of private members with the existing powers of the cabinet. It seems to me that this conflict must always exist, as it exists in the United States where even with the separation of power the congress is relatively strong.
Last night the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) mentioned that the committees of the house divide on party lines quite frequently, as of course we do in the house. He then had this to say, and I should like to quote briefly from his remarks as they appear at page 12544 of Hansard:
-because in the House of Commons we have a discipline imposed by the threat of dissolution, and this extends also to committee work, even though party divisions there may not be nearly as apparent as they would be in the house itself.
I hope they are not. Nevertheless there is always the prospect in a parliamentary committee of party divisions in the house reflecting themselves to a greater degree than they would under a congressional system.
I can assure the Prime Minister that party divisions certainly do show themselves in some committees. However, we do have some committees which are relatively non-partisan. I have been informed that the defence committee operates in that way, and the public accounts committee operates in that way; but others do not. Partisan feelings were very obvious in the flag committee, and they were certainly obvious in the committee on the Canada pension plan. During the many sessions of the Canada pension plan committee party feelings were very evident and we had many examples of Liberals and Conservatives sniping at each other. I sometimes thought that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and myself were the only ones who took a good, constructive non-partisan approach.

Since Hansard does not record facial expressions, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should add that I was smiling at that point. It is certainly possible that a committee can do good work even though partisan feelings are in evidence. In connection with the Canada pension plan committee I should add that in spite of rather bitter party fighting at times, it did a very good job and made some very good recommendations, whatever the shortcomings may have been.

I should now like to deal with several of the recommendations made by the committee on procedure and organization, and to do so I will refer to page 992 of the report of that committee where the recommendations are summarized. Item No. 6 on page 992 is:
The quorum of a standing committee, like the quorum of a special committee, should consist of a majority of the members.
I cannot disagree with that statement, but it seems very strange to me that we should demand a much higher quorum for a committee than we do for the house. If we had to have the majority of the members in the house at all times we would very rarely have a quorum after the question period.
Item No. 7 on the same page is a very good recommendation. It is this;
Provision should be made for the appointment of alternate members to committees.
I have thought of this recommendation in relation to the sessions of the Canada pension committee, some of which were held during the Christmas recess at which time some of the members of the committee had to be away from Ottawa. Had such a rule been in existence at that time, before we adjourned in December we could have designated alternate members. For example, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) was the only member of that committee representing his party. He attended as often as he could but he had to be in his constituency for at least part of the recess. During the recess we could not appoint alternate members. This certainly is a good recommendation.
Items Nos. 8 and 9 appearing at page 992 are as follows:
8.	With specified exceptions, each member should serve on at least one of the nine standing committees on legislation and estimates.
9.	With specified exceptions, each member should serve on one of the other six standing committees or as an alternate member of one of the nine standing committees on legislation and estimates.
I was pleased that the committee used the word "should" rather than the word "must" because while it is probably very useful for every member of the house to have experience on one or more committees, there are members who have neither the inclination nor the ability to serve on committees, so this should not be obligatory.
Item No. 14 states:
The house should adjourn at regular intervals for periods of two weeks at a time, during which committees would meet and members would attend to constituency duties in their ridings.
Others have commented on this particular recommendation and I should like to say that

without following it to the letter I hope something of that sort will be implemented before very long. This question of appointing time during which hon. members may leave Ottawa, yet be faithful in their attendance in the house, is a very difficult one, particularly for members who come from distant constituencies. Even though air travel is very fast, it is very difficult to make a long journey. In my case it takes a day to travel from here to the west coast and a day to return, so it is difficult for me to be in the house as much as I would like. This is a very good recommendation. I believe the Australian parliament follows a similar practice and I should like to see some variation of it put into practice here.
Item No. 16 states:
Members should be required to attend the meetings of committees to which they have been appointed.
I agree that they should be required to attend these meetings, but I do not know quite how this is going to be enforced. We have a rather loose system for enforcing attendance in the house and I do not think that problem can be solved until we solve the problem in respect of attendance in the house itself.
Item No. 19 states:
Not more than 20 days should be set aside for debating the estimates in committee of supply.
I think that is unrealistic, Mr. Speaker, even though certain standing committees would consider the estimates of various departments. I cannot conceive that all these estimates could be passed in the house in 20 days. I do not think anyone wants to take the position that committees should have the final authority in respect of estimates. That being the case, and in view of the variety of operations of the government and its many departments and crown corporations, with 265 members in the house it seems unrealistic to expect that 20 days would be a sufficient time for the estimates, even considering the amount of work that would be done by the committees.
I should like to quote briefly from recommendation 22 which appears on page 989 of Votes and Proceedings:
In order to eliminate delays and the necessity for numerous routine reports, your committee recommends that all the powers a committee is likely to need should be delegated to it when it is first appointed.
It goes on to suggest that committees should have the power to bring persons to Ottawa to appear before them and also the power to sit in other parts of Canada in order to carry
Procedure Committee Report on investigations. I can imagine that the people in charge of the budget are having nightmares over that recommendation and are thinking of the congressional junkets in the United States. However I think the idea is a good one and the power need not be abused.
But when the committee says that committees should have all the powers necessary, I am wondering whether this means they should also have the necessary research staff. The subject of research help for members and for committees has been mentioned before and the problem is a very real one. I have been a member of many committees, such as the one on railways, canals and telegraph lines and the sessional committee on the C.N.R. and Air Canada, where various experts have appeared and usually the contest has been a very unequal one. On one side you have a crown corporation with the president, numer-out vice presidents, directors and a host of expert people. Usually the average member is really quite ill equipped to do a good job of questioning. Occasionally there are members who have particular knowledge of the field under discussion and can do a very good job, but this is just a matter of luck. Normally all a member has at his disposal is the report of the particular agency, plus his newspaper clippings and speeches he has saved. He certainly cannot do the job that should be done.
The same thing is true in the house. When the estimates of various departments are being considered a member cannot do the kind of job he should do. I thought of that last year when the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce came before the house. I looked across at the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who we will all admit is very competent. He had his experts with him and in the gallery there were more experts from the various branches of the department. I felt rather unequal to the task that had been allotted to me by my party.
So I hope that the reference to powers in recommendation 22 envisages the committees branch being developed so that there will be people with expert technical knowledge available to all committees. Otherwise we will go on as in the past and the job of investigation and scrutiny that should be done will not be done. If these changes are not made, one will have to conclude that the executive does not want them to be made. As I said earlier, this is usually the attitude taken by the executive because any increase in the strength of members and in their

Procedure Committee Report knowledge and effectiveness reduces the power of the executive.
Unless some real change can be made it seems to me that one must ask the question: What is the value of parliamentary committees? In this connection I think we have much more to learn from the United States than from the United Kingdom. One of the participants at last summer's Couchiching conference, sponsored by the Canadian institute of public affairs, was a lecturer from the London school of economics, Dr. Bernard Crick. According to him the House of Commons of the United Kingdom is not much more effective than our house from the point of view of the private member or of committee work. In the Toronto Globe and Mail of July 27, 1964, there is an article headed, "U.K. House in Morass: Professor". I should like to quote some of the remarks he made in an interview at Geneva park.
If one looks at the cabinet, the government in general and the whole apparatus of the executive including the civil service, one sees constant change and improvement. But if one looks at poor old parliament it can be said without too much exaggeration that there have been no fundamental changes in its method of operation since 1908.

speechtext:
It is the very opposite. It would convert the generalities and the basic general philosophy of the report into concrete propositions that could be dealt with item by item by the House of Commons. If the session should end before the committee is able to report back to the House of Commons, the committee could quite easily be reconstituted, as it has been once before, and the entire body of evidence and the recommendations so far adopted by that committee could be accepted by the same committee so reconstituted in a new session of the House of Commons.
When one comes to deal with the specific items of the report I suppose there is not a member of the house who would be in total agreement with each one of them. There are items with regard to which I would respectfully disagree, but with the basic motive of the committee report I am heartily in agreement and I have nothing but admiration for the chairman and members of the subcommittee who have brought it forward for

[DOT]discussion in the house. I want to deal in a broad way with the general substance of the report. It is set out at the beginning where the committee says:
X. Your committee is of the opinion that the potential value of the committee system of the House of Commons is not being exploited to the full-
2. Your committee, through its subcommittee on committees, has examined a number of reforms relating to the committee structure of the house-
It will be my argument, in the few moments I have at my disposal, that the position of individual members of parliament, whether in opposition or on the government benches, can be strengthened by a strengthening of the committee system. I think we should look at the role of the member of parliament in this House of Commons, and indeed in the role of a member of parliament in a parliamentary democracy. What should he do? Ideally he should translate the wishes of his electors into debate, into action on the floor of the House of Commons. At the same time he should lead opinion, if he can, in his riding. He should be an influence upon his electorate. He should contribute toward the formation of a collective opinion in the area of the country which he is called upon to represent. In other words he is the liaison between the people and, if I may call it that, the establishment or the bureaucracy.
Now, the member of parliament, in my opinion, is the linchpin in our entire parliamentary democracy. It is he who represents the people who elected him, and because that is so it is essential to the good working of the parliamentary system that he have an effective role. There are severe limitations on the role of an individual member of parliament, no matter on which side of the house he may sit. First of all, I suppose the principle of collective responsibility of the cabinet is bound to have a restrictive effect upon his effectiveness. By "collective responsibility" I mean the doctrine under parliamentary tradition that the cabinet stands or falls as a unit. If a minister is challenged on a matter of government policy, the cabinet stands behind him and will stand or fall with him. As a result of that collective responsibility, there is always the threat of dissolution, always the threat of an election. This means, to a certain extent, that the cabinet has a leverage over the House of Commons because of this perpetual threat of dissolution and, to that extent, is immune from parliamentary control except on issues of crisis.
Procedure Committee Report
I am not questioning the cabinet form of government. It is a necessary part of the urge for efficiency in a parliamentary process and in the management of the business of the country. All I am saying is that perhaps the management or efficiency side of the house outweighs the democratic impulse of the house as expressed through the role of the individual member of parliament.
There are further restrictions on the role of the individual member, Mr. Speaker. These are caused by party discipline and by party organization. A century ago in the United Kingdom and in Canada a private member was generally free to defy his party whip or the disciplinary agent of his party. It was this independence of the ordinary member of parliament that gave the House of Commons its place of importance in public opinion. It was this independence that was the best check on the government of the day. Richard Crossman, who is now a minister in the labour government of the United Kingdom, once wrote that the prime responsibility of a member is less to his conscience and electors than to his party, because without accepting the discipline of his party he cannot be elected and if he defies that discipline he risks political death. I believe he overstates the case. The point I want to make is that the necessary efficiency of parliamentary government inflicts certain limitations on the role of the member. Here again there has to be a proper balance. If there were no cohesion of views, if those of us who are in the political system did not link ourselves toward common ends under a common leadership and contend under an adversary system with those of opposing points of view, there would be chaos. In other words, under a system of one man one vote, you would have anarchy as they did under that system in the third and fourth French republics.
This fact of party decisions being taken in caucus has, to a certain extent, made the role of the members of parliament on the floor of the House of Commons less important than it once was. The real struggles for power are today less on the floor of the House of Commons than within the party caucus. I see the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) smiling at me. He knows, from personal experience, just what I mean. The caucus of the government party and the caucus of the official opposition party have become, to a certain extent, the chief battlefields of politics, and to that extent democracy has become invisible. The struggles are carried on behind closed doors. The point is,

Procedure Committee Report how long can democracy remain invisible? How long can these struggles remain hidden from public scrutiny and still conform to the principles of democracy?
I said that the party discipline argument could be exaggerated because I am sure there is in the conscience of every member in this chamber a point where the principles for which he stands and the loyalties to which he adheres, would dictate that on specific issues important enough to him or to his electors, he would rebel against his party. This still happens, and it will continue to happen. It does not happen as often as it used to happen. As the political party becomes more organized and more discipline is required, the backbencher on either side of the house becomes more restricted.
I should like to mention a third force restricting the independent role of a member of parliament. I refer to the permanent establishment of government, the civil service, the bureaucracy or what I once was bold enough to call "the mandarin class". I may say quite clearly this is not an attack on the civil service, because all of us realize we need an efficient civil service which gives us again the balance of efficiency on the one hand against what we represent on the other, the impulse of freedom and the democratic voice. Democracy may flounder from time to time when the country is undecided or confused about issues. This indecision, this confusion, will be reflected in the House of Commons; but because of the efficiency represented by the civil service, the permanent establishment of government, the daily business of government will continue. However, today the power of the permanent civil service, the concept of efficiency, in my opinion outweighs the impulse of freedom as represented by the individual member of parliament. What we need is an effective counterbalance in this chamber in the form of an effective member of parliament. The average member is faced with a monopoly of information, as the last speaker mentioned, in the hands of the government, backed by the expertise of officialdom. There is this monopoly of information and technical competence that he, himself, cannot match except from time to time when the subject matter falls within his own competence, perhaps gained before being given his mission to this chamber by the people.
As governments increase their intervention in our society, with economic planning, five year plans, transportation legislation, pension plans and so on, the technical background


needed by each one of us for intelligent criticism becomes more complicated. The member of parliament finds the monopoly of technical information in the civil service. It is our duty here, as representatives of a working democracy, to restore the balance between freedom and efficiency. It is within this context that I view the committee's report, because by strengthening the committees system we will by my submission, strengthen the role of the individual member of parliament and allow him to compete against the restrictions of cabinet government, the restrictions of party discipline, the restrictions a monopoly of information in the hands of the permanent establishment of government may place upon him.
It is for this reason that I support heartily the committee's report to the extent that it recommends the strengthening of the committees system. It means we shall establish a procedure whereby legislation can be submitted at an earlier stage to standing and special committees of the commons for scrutiny by members. This reform would, in my opinion, achieve two main results. First, it would allow an individual member of parliament access to information upon which to base intelligent criticism. Before entering the committee he may not have had this information at his disposal. As a result of his power on that committee he will be able to call witnesses either from the civil service or from outside government to give him the information and the documentation on the basis of which he can make decisions. Evidence from civil servants and others summoned before the committee to testify as to the facts concerning the proposed legislation will make each member of the committee a more intelligent critic. In other words, the monopoly of information of which I have spoken would be broken.
The second result of this reform would, I suggest, be this: A member sitting on a committee is relatively freer of party discipline than he is when sitting and speaking in this chamber. He is freer from the lash of the party whip. Thus it is that certain committees have been conducted in a very non-partisan way. With the encouragement and extension of this system a member would have more scope to use his own judgment and talents and would be less restricted by his commitments to his party.
This report of the committee of which Your Honour is the chairman has as its motive the finding of ways in which to speed up and modernize the work of this house. This is

all to the good. It means that we who have the good fortune and the honour to be elected to represent our fellow citizens may accomplish more for the country. I wish to suggest, however, that this is not the entire solution- the streamlining of business and the modernization of procedure. We must not only get more business done here in Ottawa but we must ensure that the ordinary member of parliament who is the linchpin of democracy makes a better individual contribution to the work of the house. We must ensure that there is not only a more efficient transaction of our business but also a more democratic transaction of our affairs.
