I wish to comment briefly on some of the remarks which have been made, because I am disturbed by the suggestion that acceptance of the motion moved by the President of the Privy Council would have the effect of killing both the report and the committee for the present session. I hope it will allay some of the fears of members of this house if I deal with this and say that if the report is referred back to the committee the subcommittee is prepared to begin its meetings again on Monday to work out specific proposals based on the debate which has taken place in this chamber.
This special committee on procedure and organization is not a committee which was set up by the government. It is an all-party committee which was set up by this house. The report which was brought in was the result of a great deal of study. We did come up with a certain new concept of what should be done to deal with the estimates of expenditure. We went about as far as we could go in devising ways and means of doing this in the absence of some guidance from the house. In the course of the last two days some useful suggestions and comments have been made and the committee can take these into consideration when it begins its meetings next week, and revise its proposals accordingly. We hoped there would be this kind of discussion and comment from hon. members and I am satisfied that a large number of very useful suggestions have been made. We could try to work these into specific proposals in a new report to this parliament, but I suggest that the only way in which the committee would really be competent to do this would be if the motion moved by the President of the Privy Council were accepted. It would be difficult to proceed if the fifteenth report were still standing in our routine proceedings as well as, possibly, an eight-
Procedure Committee Report eenth report. It would be necessary to get rid of one of them in some way. The best way to do that would be to accept the motion before us. I might point out that citation 322 of Beauchesne's fourth edition states the following:
It is not competent for a committee to reconsider and reverse its own decision, but if the house resolves that such reconsideration is necessary, the correct procedure is for the house to give the committee instructions which will enable it to consider the whole question again.
Thus, if we are to achieve what I am sure most members desire, that is, a reconsideration of the recommendations, there is no other way in which to achieve this except by accepting the motion put forward by the President of the Privy Council allowing the committee to be re-activated with at least some kind of instructions. So I hope there will be no misconception of what this amendment would do. The committee will certainly get back to work very quickly and try to come forward with further specific recommendations before the end of this session. Even if we are not able to complete the work within that time we have a firm undertaking from the government that the committee will be set up again very early in the next session and we can complete the recommendations then.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should like to make a few brief remarks in connection with this report and indicate my attitude with respect to the fears which have been expressed, that if this amendment moved by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) is carried the whole cause of parliamentary reform will be dealt a damaging if not a fatal blow.
First, I think the house generally appreciates the necessity of undertaking fundamental changes in the procedure we have been following. In fact it may be true that the house is behind public opinion in coming to grips with a necessity for parliamentary reform. The committee on procedure has put forward a package of proposals, each element in the package being related to the other, and the package in itself does constitute an important step in trying to deal with the question of parliamentary reform. The three main elements in the proposals are the allocation of 20 days to dealing with estimates, an effort to restructure and upgrade the committees system in the house, and the establishment of regular adjournment periods.
The discussion so far reinforces, I think, the necessity for the reconsideration of much of these proposals. The committee proposed

Procedure Committee Report that the estimates, or the main estimates, be considered in a period limited to 20 days. There is no explicit reference in the report to supplementary estimates and interim supply. In fact, in one part of the report the committee talks about estimates and in another part it talks about main estimates. I suggest here is one instance where reconsideration would be most useful, because the purpose of confining debate in committee of supply would be frustrated if the proposals were applied only to the main estimates and if the time formerly used on the main estimates spilled over into interim supply and supplementary estimates.
The committee, I feel, ought to be given an opportunity to clarify this particular aspect for the benefit of the house. I agree in general with the restructuring of the committees system, but I do agree with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his statement that the standing committees can never be a true substitute for the House of Commons itself. That is not the suggestion inherent in the report. The House of Commons itself must remain the main and central forum in which we operate. That does not preclude the necessity of upgrading the committees system.
That point leads me to the third aspect, namely regular adjournment periods. The purpose of having regular adjournment periods was twofold; one, to give members regular opportunities to do their constituency work -and that still is an absolutely vital part of the work of a member of parliament-and the second, of course, was to have special, regular periods when committees would sit; the house would not be sitting, members would devote themselves exclusively to committee sittings which they would be obliged to attend, and this would have the effect of upgrading the work of the committees and also reducing the necessity especially of dealing with the main estimates in committee of supply. It is obvious from the discussion so far that there is not unanimity, nor is there likely to be unanimity, on the proposal made in the committee report that we have a three weeks sitting of the house, two weeks of an adjourned house, one week devoted to committees and another to visitations to constituencies. That has been regarded as too rigid, but the principle itself is still worth thinking about. I simply want to refer members of the committee to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that he in principle agrees with this particular proposal that committee sittings also be in periods of adjournment.
[Mr. MacEachen.l
There are other variations that could be considered by the committee. I believe the time has come when we must face up to the necessity for regular adjournments of the House of Commons. Why cannot we consider further in the committee agreeing on a regular summer adjournment, a regular Easter adjournment and a regular Christmas adjournment; and then possibly a particular period that might be called a committees adjournment? This would to some extent meet the objectives proposed in the committee report without imposing the rigidity that has been alleged and which may exist. I go a little further, Mr. Speaker, and say that coupled with regular adjournment periods must be the assurance that there will be an opportunity to get the business of the house done. That is provided for, at least with respect to the main estimates, by the 20-day proposal. I suggest that if regular adjournment periods, in the way mentioned, are to succeed then this proposal must be joined and coupled with time allocation in connection with principal debates of the house. Freedom of speech must be maintained, but I think our experience this session ought to have taught us that the length of time spent on a particular measure does not necessarily ensure that a good, effective and useful debate has taken place.
Mr. Speaker, we in the government are serious about parliamentary reform. We are not supporting the amendment moved by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mc-Ilraith) with the purpose of abandoning parliamentary reform; rather, we hope we can get this report sent back to the committee today. The committee could then get busy and bring back a report at the earliest possible moment incorporating at least the recommendations in this report that have common support. I suggest that the alternative is to continue the debate indefinitely; if the main motion for concurrence were put to the house it is doubtful whether it would pass. The quickest way to get an agreed solution is to get this report back to the committee for a speedy report, if possible, and then deal as quickly as possible with the further report. I want to reply to the Leader of the Opposition in that respect, who had the view that the idea of the government was to abandon this question. That is not the intention, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could ask the minister whether, as a scholar of political economy, as he is recognized to be, he can really find any justification for the

exclusion by paragraph 17 of the fifteenth report of the committee of certain members of the House of Commons from committees. The question that is in my mind is this: It appears to me that as members of parliament we in a sense should be equal. If in the wisdom of a particular parliament certain members, be they cabinet ministers, the leader of the opposition, the whip of the government or the opposition, should be deemed by their peers to be useful committee men for certain purposes, does the minister really feel that by class they should be excluded from participation in these committees?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the committee intended to discriminate against the leader of the opposition or ministers. But certainly this is not a matter that ought to divide us. If the view is that all members of parliament should still be allowed to sit on committees, I am sure the committee on procedure would have no difficulty in rewriting that section of the report.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as often happens in the House of Commons, there has been a turn of events that had not been anticipated. My understanding some time ago was the same as that of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith), that in response to requests from the members of the committee
Procedure Committee Report on organization and procedure one day would be set aside for a discussion of their report, and that was yesterday. It was our understanding that that would be all we would have time for in this particular session of the House of Commons. But apparently there has been an insistence on the part of the members of that committee to have a further discussion of their committee's report, or have some conclusion reached immediately. Therefore a compromise was attempted by the government house leader, that we would ask to have the report referred back to the committee for further study. This did not pass immediately, and the result is that that motion has been debated this afternoon and there is not now time to go on to the business we had anticipated for today, namely Bill No. C-142.
The only reason I am entering into the debate at this time is this. After listening carefully to what was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) last night, by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) today and by the chairman of the subcommittee, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), I have reached the conclusion that unless people express their opinions with regard to this report now the subcommittee, which is going to go to work Monday, so says the chairman, will base its further report or conclusions on what has been said in this chamber, and accept that as the consensus of the House of Commons.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Which is not right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well, I cannot accept that conclusion from what has happened so far. I hope that other members will have the chance to express their opinions before the subcommittee attempts to draw up any further recommendations. Because if the subcommittee is simply going to draw up its recommendations on what has been said by those who have spoken up to this point, then not all of the ground has been covered.
I think this is a bad turn of events indeed, and I think it is bad for this reason. I appreciate the difficulties facing the government house leader. I have been through the mill on that job myself. When his timetable is upset it is then very difficult to get the session back on the rails; and his timetable has now been upset by the insistence of a subcommittee of the rules and procedure committee whose object, so they tell us, is to reform parliament. These people will not even co-operate with the government house leader in his very difficult task of trying to

Procedure Committee Report get the business processed in the limited number of days ahead of him. These people are all for a reform of parliament, yet they cannot give him some assistance now in the practical management of this house. They have advanced quite a bit of theory, but I suggest to the members of that committee that you have to use some practical common sense in conducting the business of this house. I think in this instance they have not been fair to the government house leader.
Before they reach their conclusions, Mr. Speaker, if they start again on Monday, I should like them to consider some other aspects of the whole question of the rules and procedure of this house. We have heard from members of the committee who have worked on this problem, and from others, and we have read articles in the press and even heard a quotation today from somebody in another country. It is sort of common talk that there is something wrong with parliament and that public opinion is dissatisfied with parliament. Even the Minister of Labour suggested this afternoon that fundamental changes-"fundamental" changes, mark you-had to be made in parliament, and he said-these are his words-that perhaps we are behind public opinion with regard to reform.
The public should be interested in parliament, very properly so, and it does show a great deal more interest now than it did years ago. This is thanks to a number of factors: the rather disturbed world in which we are living, internationally; to better means of communication, television and radio as well as a good press in the country; and to the fact that there has been a fair bit of political turmoil in Canada for the last several years. So there is much more public attention centred on parliament than there was when I first came here 14 years ago. And this is all to the good.
However, it does not follow that because public opinion is centred on this institution we have immediately to make changes. What does this institution exist for? It has been developed over centuries. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) mentioned today, this is the year in which people interested in parliamentary government celebrate the 700th year of the existence of parliamentary institutions. It has a long and honourable history. Parliament has evolved as a method of giving the people in a democracy the means of arranging for their own government, of checking the administration of that government, deciding how much they are going to

be taxed and investigating how their taxation money is spent. This is done through debate in the House of Commons, as the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) pointed out in an article in a newspaper-I read the article before I realized who had written it; otherwise I might not have read it-we have exchanged the hurling of epithets across the floor of this chamber for the striking of blows, which is exactly what has happened. So that force does not rule; we attempt instead to govern ourselves by means of reasoned and logical argument. We are satisfied not to strike blows and bear people down by brute force but rather to engage in discussion. This is what parliament is. The freedom of this country is maintained in its parliament.
Why do people say that fundamental changes are required? This disturbs me very much. Fundamental changes would mean a change in something which has been established by trial and error over a long period of time. It is not sacred. It is not important merely because seven centuries have elapsed in the evolution of this system. But just because it is old and ancient is no reason for suddenly having to make fundamental changes. People talk glibly about the fact that we are living in a new age. It is a new age from the standpoint of technological improvement, of course it is; and our living conditions have changed beyond all knowledge. They are quite different from what previous generations had to endure. But the method of debate has not changed. The rules of debate do not need much modification from one century to another. You determine how long a person may speak and whether he gets his chance in turn with others who also want to speak, and so on. Are we going to make fundamental changes in the rules of debate? I think that is nonsense.
Therefore I question the use of the expression "fundamental changes in parliament". I do not want to see fundamental changes in an institution which has proved its worth. As the Leader of the Opposition reminded us, it has proved its worth in time of war and time of emergency.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question. I am not quite clear what he means by fundamental changes. Is he suggesting that the kind of changes in the rules of debate that the British and other parliamentary systems have instituted in past years are not of a fairly important nature?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIFTEENTH REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was criticizing the expression used by the Minister of Labour

(Mr. MacEachen), so that question should be addressed to him. What does he mean by "fundamental changes"? I can see certain small changes taking place from time to time, improving conditions here as a result of some of the methods perhaps getting out of date, or because they are not satisfactory. I could suggest offhand certain minor changes-I would not call them fundamental-with regard to questions of privilege and things of that nature; but what did the minister mean by "fundamental changes"?
I think the committee on rules and procedure started off from the wrong premise. It started off with the idea that reform of parliament was necessary. I sometimes think it started off with the idea of change for the sake of change. That committee worked on the basis that there was something wrong with parliament. Parliament is fulfilling its function. It does not operate in quite the same way each year, because this depends on the composition of the house, the strength of the government and the opposition, and on the number of parties in the house. It does operate from year to year in somewhat different ways.
The multiplicity of parties in a house changes the temper of a house and changes to a certain extent the modes of progression in a house. I have seen that happen and so have you, Mr. Speaker, during the time you have been here. We have to adjust ourselves to that fact. The people through their voting power have decided that there should be quite a number of parties in the House of Commons. As one of my colleagues pointed out the other night, the House of Commons reflects to a certain extent instability, if you like, in political life in Canada. That instability is manifested by the multiplicity of parties here. The public having made that decision with regard to the composition of this house has to put up with the situation here, and may find that things do not go along quite as smoothly or as rapidly as they might if we had a two-party system with a government and an opposition.
The committee started from the wrong premise and it reached the conclusion that great changes had to be made. The committee in its report has argued that there would be a substantial improvement in this house if the committees system was thoroughly overhauled. The first sentence of their report has been read, but I will read it again. It is this:
Your committee is of the opinion that the potential value of the committee system of the House of Commons is not being exploited to the full- 20220-797
19, 1965
Procedure Committee Report
We have heard various members of this house state that there should be an expansion of the committees system and that committees should be given more power. The hon. members of the N.D.P. who have spoken so far lean toward the congressional system in existence in the United States and favour that committee system which formulates policy and attempts to get the administration to accept it, or which rejects policy put forward by the administration, or modifies it. That is the republican form of government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) referred to it in his speech last evening. It is not a parliamentary system, and I hope that when the special committee commences its work again it will not try to put powers for formulating policy in the hands of the committees of this house. I object to that because it is wrong and because it does not fit in with a parliamentary system.
The committee makes a great point about the fact that an expansion of our committees system would be excellent for individual members because they would have more to do. Some people suggest that the individual member of parliament does not have enough to do and that by increasing the number of committees they will then be able to keep themselves occupied. I think the situation which faces any member of this House of Commons at any time is that without any committee work whatsoever a member of parliament has more to do than he can adequately accomplish.
I see no limit to what a member of the House of Commons can do by way of informing himself and participating on occasion in the debates of this house without any need for multiplying the number of committees, but this again depends on the individual. With 20 departments of government to examine, any member who comes to this House of Commons can in the course of time become reasonably expert and proficient in respect of one or two of these fields of activities. We do not have to have committees in order to accomplish that purpose.
The one value of the committees of the House of Commons not mentioned by the rules and procedure committee is that the committees may bring before them officials and experts from which the individual member of parliament can obtain information rather quickly. The committees do not exist just for the purpose of supplying members with information. The value I see in committee work is related to the fact that administrators in the civil service, or public service, have to come

Procedure Committee Report and give an accounting of their trusteeships to members of parliament. My experience with people in those capacities has been that they rather welcome the opportunity of explaining what they are doing and this applies to departments of government and crown corporations, unless of course they are being harassed toy committee members. Senior members of the civil service have told me that an appearance before a parliamentary committee is good for them and for their associates in the departments, because it keeps them on their toes. They know from year to year that what they are doing may be examined very carefully by a committee of the house. That is a useful and purposeful type of committee work.
Whether or not members can obtain information and knowledge through committee work depends entirely on the individual member. I have attended many committees and I know the frustration of members. I listened to all the praises of the defence committee. I served on that defence committee for a year and I know that there was no influencing of government policy by that committee. In fact, the minister said he did not want us to tell him what to do in the way of policy. There was a great deal of expert information given by officials of the Department of National Defence, but with 24 members on the committee the restriction in respect of questions is great. An hon. member may ask one question or one supplementary question, and then the ball passes to someone else who in turn asks one question or a supplementary question. With 24 members sitting around a table questioning an admiral or a general the opportunity of a committee member to obtain information is restricted to one question per meeting, or perhaps not even that.
I am not impressed by the laudatory phrases which have been used as to how valuable the work of a committee is, or by the suggestion that members can ask questions and ferret out information. I have been on too many committees to accept that statement without a grain of salt. There is some value in gaining information from some of these committees, but there is some difficulty in getting on them. In the first seven years I was here I would have liked to be on the external affairs committee, but there was a tight little corporate body that controlled the membership of that committee. I was not put on it, except for two days on one occasion, because I had made a special study of the subject of genocide and the external affairs committee was discussing that matter.
IMr. Churchill.]
But after the two days were over I was shuffled off again and nevermore appeared. So there is some difficulty in getting on some of these so-called elite committees. I got information on external affairs by reading all the committee reports and everything else I could lay my hands on with regard to international affairs, and any member of the House of Commons can do the same thing. So you do not actually have to serve on a committee.
I want to deal with something in the report which I think strikes at the root of our freedom of speech here, and would be very bad if introduced as a recommendation by the subcommittee next week or the following week. It is something which seemed to get the approval of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) this afternoon and perhaps of some others. I refer to how we are to deal with the main estimates in the House of Commons.
As I see the work of the House of Commons, our main job when we come here is really the budget, or how much taxation is to be imposed on the Canadian people. That is our main purpose. That is why parliament was assembled in the early days. The second purpose is to see how the taxation money is spent, and the third purpose is the passing of useful legislation. You can put all three on much the same level but I do not by any means put the budget or the main estimates in an inferior position.
The committee is likely to propose, as they have indicated in their report, that when we come to the main estimates in the House of Commons we will be restricted to 20 days. Their argument is that if the estimates are referred to committees and studied there in great detail-I have been all through this and I know how much that amounts to-we do not need to discuss them at length in the House of Commons. This is not a new idea. An estimates committee was established in former years which was very active. As a matter of fact, in 1955 six departments were referred to that committee, six in 1956, eight in 1958 and a similar number in 1959. The officials were present and were examined. That estimates committee worked well and it should have been set up again so that it could have been operating.
But the restriction to 20 days in the House of Commons will limit freedom of speech, will prevent examination of cabinet ministers to see whether they have knowledge of their departments and are good administrators and will not provide us with the opportunity to find out what their policy is with regard to

their departments. I suggested informally to the rules and procedure committee eight months ago that on a trial basis we should allow 45 days for the study of the main estimates here in the House of Commons, with the public able to be present and listen and the members of the press gallery also present. If you shift these things to committees you lose the press. They would not know where to find some of the committees in the buildings we have. Examine the estimates right here in the House of Commons. Put the ministers on the spot. We were put on the spot when we were in the government. That was all right. As a minister of the crown I welcomed it. Let us examine the ministers publicly as to their knowledge of their departments. Let us examine them with regard to the policies of their departments. It is not so much a question of finding out whether they need another $5 or $10 or $15 million, although that is important. What we want to know is whether the government is being properly conducted and whether the ministers know their jobs. This is the place to do it. Restrict us to 20 days and we are chopped off.
Normally it takes 60 days to deal with the main estimates in the House of Commons. I suggested that as an experiment for one year we should set a limit of 45 days. The committee has cut this down to 20 days. This is one of the things in the committee report to which I object. When the subcommittee is examining this matter next week I hope they will bear that in mind and not come up with such a restrictive idea which will limit debate and prevent us from doing our job.
May I add that although there may be 15, 24 or 60 members on a committee there are ether members of the house who are not on those committees and who are entitled when the main estimates come to the floor of the house to make speeches, investigate policy and ask questions. For example, the very fact that I may not be a member of the veterans affairs committee or of the defence committee or the external affairs committee should not prevent my talking on any of these three subjects in committee of supply when the minister is facing the public. I exert my right, which is that of any member of the house, to have my say with regard to some of these problems.
However, as an experiment I suggest a period of 45 days. Let the opposition select the departments it would like to deal with and at the end of the 45 days let the guillotine fall. Then there can be no complaint on the part of the opposition. But if you have a period of only 20 days the guillotine falls too 20220-7971
Procedure Committee Report soon and millions of dollars in estimates will be passed in the house without adequate discussion. We had an example of that last fall. I suggested to the government house leader and he accepted the idea that we take seven days to complete the main estimates. We did so, but as hon. members will recall the guillotine fell on Friday afternoon without the Department of Transport and other departments having been examined. Millions of dollars in estimates were put through without examination. That is a good example of what happens when you have a fixed date for the end of a debate. Anyone who was here will remember-those who were not can look at the record and see-how easily some of the ministers got off because of the guillotine falling and how little attention the house was able to give to several major departments.

For the first time the government cannot control all the committees. For the first

Procedure Committee Report time they have not been able to direct what the committees can do. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the situation has been so bad that the opposition has been responsible in many cases for seeing that quorums were arranged for committee meetings.

speechtext:
Well, you have not attended. However, we do not want to get into an argument of that kind. I have been a member for only a short period of time and since I have not seen her there I assumed she was not a member.
No cabinet wants strong committees when the government party has a large majority. I think the official opposition will agree that the question of committees did not become important until there was a minority government. Then this proposition becomes very important. It is necessary to get business done, Mr. Speaker, but have we really decided what we want to accomplish? I have been a member of many very good committees. I believe a good example is the defence committee. The defence committee is an excellent example of a committee that studies a great many matters. However, look at your newspapers, look at the announcements of changes in defence policy that have been made in the house, and you will find that none of them has been referred to this particular committee. The recommendations a committee makes are never taken into consideration. There is no way in which our committees can become part of the legislative branch. Unless we are willing to give some legislative responsibilities to committees so that the cabinet will have to make a decision upon whether or not they agree with the committee, there might as well not be any committees.
I have always found committees to be an exercise in futility. You can have as many IMr. Peters.]
research people as you want; you can be as smart as you want; you can know as much about the subject as you want, but when the committee present its report to the house that will be the end of the matter. speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Fisher (Port Arthur) moved
subtopic: PROVISION FOR RETRAINING AND MOVING COSTS OF DISPLACED EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-67, to amend the Railway Act (responsibility for dislocation costs).
He said: I am pleased to have this opportunity of giving the house a chance to approve a bill which has already in exactly the same form won the approval of the main committee of the house which deals with these matters, and which is actually a committee of this particular parliament.
In 1963 the committee considered the subject matter of this bill. The bill had been referred to the committee at the request of the government. This was in line with an indication of a similar course of action by the previous government when the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) was minister of transport. The bill went to the committee, hearings were held during the summer of 1963 and we heard strong representations particularly from spokesmen for the major railways, including Mr. Emerson who is now the new president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the committee approved a series of recommendations. In effect, it approved the substance of the bill.
For this reason I feel some optimism, in bringing this forward at the present time, that the bill will receive quick agreement in the house and that the general idea will be forwarded to the railways committee which at the present time is considering in an informal way, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) knows, the very act to which this is a minor amendment.

The problem which is involved in this measure has been before the house repeatedly. I am looking here at the submission made to the government of Canada by the national legislative committee of the international railway brotherhoods dated January 28, 1959. It has a section on page 8 making a recommendation almost identical with what is embodied in this bill. Actually, the railway brotherhoods first brought this idea forward in 1957 and have been advocating it for a long time. Only last week on March 11 the same group of railway brotherhoods, through their national legislative committee, made a submission to the government of Canada. I hope to read part of that submission and part of the reply given by the Minister of Transport to it. But first I thought I might make better sense out of what has transpired in the last week or two by quoting from an article which appeared in Railway Labour on August 1, 1964. The heading is: "Rail Job Security Issue Revived" and the subheading reads: "Flipflop charged to Pickersgill on Law Change." It says:
Executives of Canadian rail unions met in emergency session here last week to deal with the apparent rejection by Minister of Transport J. W. Pickersgill of a recommendation made over seven months ago by a Commons' standing committee.
That committee proposed that railway employees adversely affected by automation and technological change be compensated for their loss. The transport minister had said the recommendation was under "active consideration", but he has apparently repudiated that assurance, according to the unions.
The repudiation was seen in his response to a question put to him recently by the same committee when president Donald Gordon of the Canadian National was testifying.
m The transport minister at that time was asked: "What has happened to the recommendations of last year's committee on this matter?" He replied in part:
The principle involved here is so far reaching that I think it would be very difficult to contemplate applying very easily to the railways a principle that was not going to be applied to other aspects of the economy. This is a consequence of automation.
"I would ask myself a basic question which every member of parliament has to ask himself, whether we feel that we should attempt to make the shippers pay for something. If it is to be a social policy, perhaps it should be paid for by the taxpayers. These are some of the problems that arise in this field."
That was in August, 1964, Mr. Speaker; I want you to note that:
But two members of the committee-J. H. Horner, of Acadia, and Douglas Fisher, of Port Arthur- pointed out to Mr. Pickersgill that just such principles as these were very carefully considered by the committee during several months of hearings in 1963 that led to the following recommendation:
Railway Act
"The government shall give consideration to amending section 182 of the Railway Act to ensure the rights of railway employees in those cases where abandonment, merger or co-ordination between railways, or the closing or near-closing of terminals and shops, or the introduction of run-throughs is undertaken by the management.
"The committee would prefer that such matters as adjustment, compensation, retraining arrangements, and other ameliorations of dislocation be a matter of negotiation between management and the employees' legitimate bargaining agencies, but it recognizes that a strong encouragement to such means of settlement will ensue when section 182 is read in such a legal way as to offer firm protection to the employees."
I do not want to go into the long history of the interpretation of section 182 of the present Railway Act or the difficulties involved in section 168 of the present Railway Act; but the point is that in this Bill No. C-120 that was brought in by the government there is a deliberate-I can only assume it is deliberate -ignoring of section 182, and the only changes that are made in reference to section 186, it seems to me, relate to the abandonment of branch lines; in other words, it is to fit in with part of the policy that we are seeing in the future in western Canada. I might add, Mr. Speaker, that it seems very odd to me that the Minister of Transport can argue so vaguely against the import of this particular bill at the very same time as he is marshalling in a bill that in effect sets up a number of agencies-at least two agencies-and very large subsidies in funds in order to take care of rail line abandonment in one particular part of the country. I hope my friends from the west do not think I am against that, but I just want to make the point that if you can set up this kind of authority and make the arrangements for one section of the country to deal with one specific problem, to save communities and employees from damage, then surely it should be made universal.
Now I would like to turn to the submission of last week from the national legislative committee of the international railway brotherhoods. They say on page 1;
Since 1957 we have, in our annual briefs to the government, requested an amendment to section 182 of the Railway Act. The historical background regarding section 182 and other relevant sections have been placed before you-
That is, before the cabinet:
-on innumerable occasions, and we see no reason to repeat them all again.
The amendment we are seeking is intended to give application to the principle of compensation to railway employees who lose their employment or are required to change their residence as a result of changes beneficial to a railway.
You will recall that this matter was referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and

Railway Act
telegraph lines on June 27, 1963, on motion of a member of your cabinet.
That, of course, is the particular bill that we now have before us:
The committee held eight hearings and heard representation from representatives of all the railway brotherhoods-
Then it goes on to re-quote the recommendations that I have already read. Then later, on page 2, they say:
Subsequent to the report of the standing committee, we have requested your government to introduce legislation designed to implement the recommendation of the committee with no success to date.
On September 14, 1964, the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill introduced in the house, Bill C-120, an act designed to implement certain recommendations of the royal commission on transportation. When speaking to the resolution on the bill, the honourable minister, beginning on page 7981 of Hansard, said in part:
"With respect to what the government will be proposing, I may say that of course we are taking our responsibility as a government for the proposals in general, but it is the intention of the government to have this bill sent after second reading, provided the house sees fit to give it second reading, to the railway committee, because it is of such vast importance to everyone in the country. We think it would be quite unreasonable to take any other course. We would expect that the committee would hear representations from all seriously interested bodies."
With all due respect for the assurances given by the hon. minister in this regard, we suggest to him and to your government that we have already appeared before the railway committee, and as we have pointed out, we evidently satisfied the 60-member committee that our cause was justified, our requests reasonable, and they recommended accordingly. We have no choice but to express extreme disappointment in the fact that the committee's recommendation that section 182 be amended is not contained in Bill C-120 and we recommend that concurrent with consideration of Bill C-120, your government introduce an amendment that will implement the recommendation of the standing committee.
That can be done very easily if the government is prepared to take some action out of the opening that is offered to them today with this particular bill. I wanted, Mr. Speaker, to quote briefly from a press report the minister's reaction to these proposals by the national legislative committee. This is from the Port Arthur News-Chronicle of Friday, March 12, 1965, a story by Ben Ward to the Canadian Press. The headline is, "JobJarring Automation Under Study by Ottawa" and the article says:
Transport minister Pickersgill said Thursday the government is trying to decide who should carry the financial load of easing the job-jarring effects of automation-the companies involved or the public treasury.

This is the same pitch that he was on last August, only he is a little bit more vague now. The story goes on:
He told a delegation from the railway brotherhoods there are strong arguments on both sides of the question and the government is taking a serious look at them.
The government has been taking a serious look at them since December, 1963. How long, oh Lord, how long does it have to take a look at them? The article goes on:
The delegation, representing nine unions and 100,000 operating railway employees, asked in its brief that job protection and compensation for job dislocation be written into the railway legislation now before parliament.
The brief said many railway workers will lose their jobs and many more will be forced to move their homes when the railways are allowed to abandon money-losing lines and services. Some railway communities would be faced with "economic ruin".
Mr. Pickersgill said he sympathizes-
One of the things we are strong on here is sympathy:
-with the union's arguments and stressed that "the government has not closed its mind on this matter".
But there was some doubt whether the necessary compensation involved should be a charge on the railways-and ultimately the shippers-or be borne by the general economy.
He said the railway situation is just one part of the much larger subject of automation and its effects. He indicated the government is thinking of a general policy to apply in all such cases, not just railways.
J. S. Huneault, chairman of the delegation, said the brotherhoods "need more than just sympathy... we are looking for action".
Labour Minister MacEachen indicated that he plans to amend labour legislation later this year to make automation issues open to negotiation during the life of a contract. This is not provided in the present Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
We have had this circuitous approach to this subject under consideration for many months by this government, and for many months before that by the previous government. We have a situation where the Department of Labour is supposedly looking at it. Yet the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and his officials seem to be in conflict with the national employment service. Certainly they are in disagreement with the Canadian Labour Congress and the Economic Council of Canada over the way to approach this particular problem.
Given this kind of confusion at this stage, after months of so-called consideration of the matter, it seems to me that waiting for this government to make an over-all approach is not good enough. I appeal to the minister as a practical man, as a person who is prepared to

move in small ways or to take minor steps rather than to make any great big majestic change, to consider that this bill offers the government an opportunity to send once again the recommendations of our railway committee to the committee, with the request that they include them in their considerations and discussions of the act. One way in which I would back down from this request would be if the minister gave me the assurance that the new form of the bill which he is introducing in the next session will seriously take account of this particular point.
One last matter I might mention is this. The minister, if he does take the opportunity to make some remarks, may suggest that this bill is somewhat out of place in view of the fact that an inquiry is looking into certain matters which are partially covered by the provisions of this bill. However, I should like to make the point that if the minister has been reading the proceedings of that inquiry or the press reports, he will realize that contained in this general problem is a responsibility right across the country that is very large and great. I think the most able judge who is considering this would not feel that parliament or the committee of the House of Commons was impinging on the work he is planning to do if, during the time he is considering the material before him to reach a decision, he could hear something more definitive from this parliament or from the government as to where it stands on this particular question.
I would hope that if this bill is talked out- and we have to be realistic; it probably will be-then even then it will not be necessary to reintroduce it in a future session of this house. I hope the minister will realize that a government can in a sense posture only so long. In many ways it would be better, and certainly braver, if it just said no, instead of this continual dragging out of matters with the suggestion that perhaps they will or maybe they won't, but gosh, it's all very difficult.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR RETRAINING AND MOVING COSTS OF DISPLACED EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to speak after so decisive a speaker as the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). In his column which he writes in his other capacity, what I might call his capacity as the Dorothy Kil-gallen of our little Hollywood here, he described me the other day as a shilly-shallying, indecisive person. Perhaps it would be a mistake for me to prove him wrong by listening to the appeal he made just a few moments ago to be practical in small matters, if I 20220-798
Railway Act
could not be so in large matters, by doing something about this. But, Mr. Speaker, this is not a small matter. This bill seeks to do something which, in my view, is only one aspect-I admit a very important aspect-of what I consider the greatest problem which faces any industrial society today. I do not think there is any other problem in the world today which is more important, except the problem of maintaining the peace of the world. Because if we do not do that, these other things do not matter much. But outside of that I do not think there is anything more important than finding the right kind of answer to what is loosely called automation or technological change.
I think unemployment breeds the same kind of fears and uncertainties in men's minds as in the great depression days. Happily, so far it has not reached any proportions. In fact it has been very gratifying in the last two or three years to see that employment has been rising, that unemployment is not as great as it was, though we cannot be too satisfied with the situation as it is now. But I think the most tragic aspect of unemployment is the kind of unemployment that comes to men in their forties and fifties, men who have been faithful in doing a good job, who are established in a community, who have every normal reason to believe that their occupation is going to continue for the rest of their lives, and who suddenly find themselves, through no fault of their own whatever, without employment of the kind they have been used to, and in many cases without any satisfactory alternative, owing to a change in technology or in the method of doing things.
I do not think that this problem can be taken lightly at all, and I hope that no one thinks that I take it lightly. However, notwithstanding what the hon. member for Port Arthur has said, and notwithstanding the great respect that I have for the members of the committee who in 1963 did give, I know, serious and conscientious consideration to this matter, it is not always easy to convince the generality of the population that one aspect of a problem should be dealt with, when it is not being dealt with for other members of the population.
I know it is true that most of the occupations in this country which are affected by what we loosely call automation are not directly under the jurisdiction of this parliament; these workers are under the jurisdiction of the legislatures. We had the same problem when my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) was dealing with

Railway Act
the labour standards bill. That bill, of course, is going to affect only a very small proportion of the workers of Canada, but it is going to affect all of the workers who, as workers, come under the jurisdiction of this parliament. This bill singles out the railway employees, and not all of them. It singles out certain of the railway employees and offers them, or purports to offer them, a degree of job security which we are not giving to others who are equally under the jurisdiction of parliament. It seeks to impose the financial obligation for this job security, not upon the community generally but upon the railways; and since the railways have to try in some fashion or other to recuperate what they spend from freight rates, or possibly from passenger rates-though they do not seem to be very successful in that field-it is not financially possible. I think this is true, notwithstanding the fact that I said it last summer and again the other day. The fact that one says things twice six months apart does not make them any less true.
It is really important economically to decide whether or not we should impose a tax indirectly upon shippers in order to deal with this problem, or directly upon the generality of the community. I do not think the arguments are conclusive either way, and to that extent the hon. gentleman was quite right when he wrote the other day stating that I am indecisive. There are a great many things about which I am indecisive because I try to be honest enough not to pretend to know the answers to questions when I do not know the answers.
Frankly, if I was quite convinced that this was the proper way of dealing with this problem I would recommend it to my colleagues, and if they were agreeable to accepting it, it would be included in the railway bill when it is brought down the next time. I feel that until a little more progress has been made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) with the work he is doing in the field of automation, and until we have had an opportunity of deciding on an approach which will deal with all the aspects of this problem, we must avoid taking certain unknown steps. I think we must look at this in much the same way we considered the labour standards bill. I confess that if that can be done it would be a much preferable way of doing it, and would be fairer to everyone.
I think we can go on a little further than that, and I think I would find it very difficult to say that I could support this bill. That
[Mr. Pickersglll.l
does not mean to say that I think the hon. member is necessarily wrong. I did attempt to restore the law to what everyone believed it was, in respect of this matter, in that abortive bill which is now in a corpse-like state-and I realize that I am mixing my metaphors rather badly. In respect of the supreme court decision, it does seem to me that it did not properly construe what parliament meant the statute to mean. I hasten to say that I do not in any way wish to reflect on the judgment of the court, as I feel it was probably right in the construction of the statute. If the law should be the way it was before, then we should put it back to that.
I do not think the hon. member will entirely disagree with me when I suggest that there are many aspects of this problem involving job security which can be more effectively dealt with by collective bargaining than by the rather blunt instrument of legislation. If we did accept this bill, what we would be doing would be to instruct the board of transport commissioners to fix, without setting any real criteria, such compensation as they may deem proper for financial loss. That is not going to be a very easy thing to do, particularly for a board such as the board of transport commissioners. Is that board to deem that everyone who will be replaced, or who loses his occupation because of these changes, is going to be unemployed for the rest of his life? Is the board going to decide that a period of one year will be required and that certain moving expenses should be allowed? There are many criteria that will have to be worked out, and I am not sure that we should leave legislative provisions of that character and scope to an appointed body like the board of transport commissioners, considering the generalities of this case. I know the hon. member could well say that it is done in the cases that are already referred to in the act, but there is a fairly restricted number of them and there is a certain amount of jurisprudence in this regard.
I am trying to be quite honest about this, and I do not think that the board of transport commissioners as presently constituted would be an adequate body to deal with job security in so general a way as this.
Even if we decided that the railways should bear this cost and there should be no contribution to it by the taxpayers or the general public, I am not at all sure that we would not have to lay down criteria for such compensation in this parliament, because while it is true that railways are soulless corporations, if

you like, and it is not a good principle to
confer, whenever it can be avoided, upon anybody other than parliament the right to tax even indirectly. There is no use in pretending that the railways are going to dig up a great treasure that they have hidden somewhere and therefore will be able to pay this compensation. They are going to pass it on to the shipper, if they can. If they cannot, then of course we are going to worsen the financial position of the railways.
Quite frankly I would rather see us tackle this problem directly. I have not had a chance to speak to the Minister of Labour about this, but I hope some appropriate committee of this house such as the industrial relations committee could tackle this problem in respect of automation at the next session of parliament, finding out what is being done by the government and elsewhere, and thus airing this whole situation. I cannot think of anything else that, in human terms, is more important to deal with than this problem.
So far as I am concerned, if I felt that this was the most effective way of tackling the problem I would ask this house to pass the bill this afternoon; but I do not think it is, and I suggest I am not shilly-shallying by putting the thing off. I agree with the hon. member that Mr. Justice Freedman's inquiry is going to be very useful. It is being carried on I think by a very able man and one of the most fair jurists in Canada, who certainly is not devoid of what might be called a social conscience.

Mr. Speaker, I expect to detain the house for only a few moments, but in opening my remarks I should like to state at once that I think the minister's arguments, with all due respect to the hon. gentleman, are very weak. First of all, he did broaden the topic somewhat by bringing in automation and technological advances, commonly referred to, I believe, as cybernation, and I do not think there is any disagreement anywhere in the house that this is one of the major problems that society must face.
There is an old adage, "no work, no eat". This is not the case any more in these days of technological advances and automation. However, we are faced with this problem and one must start somewhere. If the argument put forward by the minister were one that would hold water, no progress would be made in any direction under any circumstances in dealing with legislation within this house. Somewhere along the line we are going to find inequities in what we do here, but the point is that we are moving in the right direction. With regard to the Canada pension plan the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) has made the plea over and over again that we have to start somewhere and move ahead. We are certainly not going to achieve something that will end all problems. There are going to be inequities. On that basis the minister's argument is of no value at all in dealing with the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) which is now before us.
By way of argument the minister said that attention must be paid to the principle of compensation. I want to say that this principle is already in the act. The principle of compensation to employees is spelled out, not in connection with the loss of wages but with regard to other aspects of the economic wellbeing and welfare of the individual. So I must say that the minister's argument is very weak.

There is also the fact that the national railroads are being compensated to a degree from the federal treasury and therefore the whole burden does not necessarily fall on the railway companies. In addition, I think this amendment would be an incentive to both employees and employers with respect to retraining programs which would restore individuals to gainful employment. Mr. Speaker, I must say that I wish I had today's Hansard in front of me because I should very much like to be able to quote to the Minister of Transport some of the brave words he uttered at about five o'clock this afternoon with regard to the desire of himself and the government for action, and to draw a contrast between those remarks and the kind of action he was prepared to see taken with regard to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher).
I certainly agree with the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) that in dealing with problems of this kind we have to start somewhere, and the bill before us does present a specific means of dealing with what I think we all recognize is an urgent and specific problem with specific application in the railways field. I listened to what the hon. member for Port Arthur said in introducing his bill and at no time did I hear him suggest that the measure he is proposing to meet this problem is necessarily the final solution to the broad problems of automation to which the minister referred. For that reason I certainly cannot agree with the minister's contention that we must put off any action until we have finally made up our minds as to how we are going to cope with the broad problems of automation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair in any way and I do not think that is quite a correct interpretation of my point. I think my point was that if we can find some way not only of dealing with all the problems of automation but of dealing with all workers under the jurisdiction of this parliament, by one measure, it would be desirable to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite glad to accept the minister's correction but I think my basic argument still stands. I will alter it to say that I do not think we need to sit back and wait until we have devised ways and

means of dealing with the problems of all of the workers under federal jurisdiction before we deal with this kind of problem. At this particular juncture in time I believe the effect of automation is bearing down with greater severity on this particular segment of the working people under federal labour jurisdiction than it is on any other. Perhaps the kind of experience we might gain out of what may not be a complete proposal for all the problems would give us some indication of where we should go in developing broader policies.
When I heard the hon. member for Port Arthur ejaculate in the course of his remarks, "Oh Lord, how long?", I was reminded of the fact that the very first motion which ever appeared in my name on the order paper of the house had reference to this very problem. It is quite true that the Minister of Transport was not the minister then-I am referring to 1953 or 1954-but he was a member of the then government. When we talk about length of consideration I respectfully suggest to him that if he has not had this problem under consideration for at least that long it is my humble view, as the introducer of that resolution, that he should have had it under consideration for that long, although not continuously, of course. While the proposal I advanced may not have been a complete answer to the problem, nevertheless it was a proposal which, if it had been taken up and developed by the government of the day could have created a situation where the machinery would have been created to deal with this problem of the dislocation of railway workers.
My proposal at that time was that, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider setting up a form of national insurance which would be universally applicable. If some development along this line had been followed the railways, as one segment of our economy, would have been making a fair contribution into some such national fund and this problem of whether or not the whole load in a particular situation should fall upon the railways, to which the minister referred, would not now be a problem. Apparently it is a problem that has been distressing him over a period of many months. I am quite prepared to accept the fact the minister is concerned about this problem, and it is a complicated one. Having listened to what the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said, and the kind of reply made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), I could

not refrain from rising and saying briefly that I echo his sentiments of, how long, oh Lord, before we get the kind of action that is required?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RETRAINING AND MOVING COSTS OF DISPLACED EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
In the few
minutes left I think we can get right to the basic problem at issue in this bill, that is the problem of who should be responsible for people who are displaced or lose their employment as a result of some form of change. Obviously, I believe everyone in the house feels that somebody should accept this responsibility. The argument is, should that responsibility rest on the state or should it rest on the company? The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), in his column and in discussing the bill, indicated that the minister tended to shilly-shally or be indecisive on this question. The minister has the burden of responsibility in connection with this problem. The hon. member for Port Arthur and I do not have responsibility for the action that is to be taken to meet this problem. We can, therefore, afford the luxury of being a little more decisive.
I have made up my mind about this question. I feel that this bill should not pass because I do not think the railways or any commercial corporation should be saddled with the problems caused by unemployment, which is a general problem. Here we are dealing only with the railways, but this problem has general application throughout industry. We have to bear that in mind. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) suggested we have to start somewhere. This is true, we do have to start somewhere. However, when we start I think we have to make sure we are starting down the right path. I feel it is very important that whatever precedent we first set be the right precedent, because the action that is taken will probably set the pattern that develops later. If we adopt a precedent here to the effect that the railways are responsible, it may be a precedent that will follow throughout every industry.
Let us look at the specific things we have to do when somebody is put out of work as a result of change. The first thing we have to do is to find some means of supporting that person and his family during the dislocation period. The next thing we have to do is ascertain what possible jobs this man might take. We have to know what his potential skills are. We have to know what skills are in demand in the country and where they are in demand. Having ascertained that, we can then start a process of retraining this person to qualify
Business of the House for the skills that are needed. Having done that, having retrained the individual, you then have to make some provision for the individual to move to where the job may be. This may involve the cost of moving his family, disposing of a house, getting a new place to live, and so on.
I cannot believe that throughout the whole country, throughout the whole of industry, private industry is the best mechanism for coping with this sort of problem. In the railway industry, we happen to have a board, as the minister indicated, which could be used to resolve this sort of problem. Let us translate this to other segments of industry- not the railways, but private commercial corporations. To whom would they turn to make decisions about compensation? To whom would they turn for a decision about retraining? They have nobody to whom to turn. I think the only way we can deal with this sort of problem is to accept this as a national or governmental responsibility. There is no doubt that in the past the trend in dealing with unemployment has been toward retraining. We have also tended to try to move jobs to people, which is also a good scheme.
I believe that sooner or later we are going to have to face the fact that if we are going to have full employment in the country we are going to have to move people to the jobs that exist; we are going to have to do a much better job of knowing what jobs exist now, what jobs are likely to exist in the future. I believe these are functions of the Department of Labour in this country, rather than of private industry, as this bill would indicate. I feel this bill would set a precedent which is wrong. I would much sooner see activity and effort on the part of our Department of Labour to build up the sort of services that will be required so we can cope with this type of problem, not only in the railway industry, not only in the one small segment of the economy, but cope with this problem nationally in all parts of the country.
May I call it six o'clock?
